@@134928095 <h> Conservatives offer little in binding Canadians to a common cause <p> Having lived in almost every province in Canada while being an Air Force brat , I 've often been confronted with the need to reassess my opinions as to how segregated populations develop their political philosophies . Fortunately , this " travelling " experience has allowed me to be exposed to an equally diverse range of political contributors , including former Prime Ministers ( St. Laurent , Pearson , Diefenbaker and PET ) , premiers ( Allan Blakeney , Rene Levesque and Wab Kinew ) , royalty ( Princess Ann ) and international leaders ( Gerald Ford and Marshall Tito among them ) . <p> Now , if you foolishly want to believe that I 'm offering up this list of dignitaries just to brag , you 're already missing the point of this column , which is that were it not for the fact that my father happened to be posted at one of these locations where an historical event was about to unfold -- OR I was trying to freelance a story so that I could @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ these encounters would ever have happened . Then I would n't have had " learning experiences " to share with those who regularly read my column . <p> Right now , though , I 'm trying to expand that readership to include more rural folk , simply because my mother was a descendent of Ukrainian immigrants who came to Canada to escape the Bolshevik 's version of Marxist theology being applied to their daily lives . @@134962740 <h> Ontario woman 's 1,300 bags of garbage tell a story of pollution , climate change and the Great Lakes <p> Grand Bend resident Lynn Tremain stood at the edge of Pinery Provincial Park , gazing out over Lake Huron as its endless blue steadied her racing thoughts . Less than 10 percent is recycled while over 175 thousand tonnes is exported to countries like the U.S. , India , Thailand and Malaysia . <p> " The rest still ends up somewhere " within our country , Lynn noted . <p> In March 2021 , when many Ontarians turned to online grocery pickup during the pandemic , she was one of them . Soon , she watched unwanted single-use plastic , which she had long avoided using , stack up in her home . <p> " I was horrified by that , " she recalled . <p> The International Solid Waste Association estimated that single-use plastic consumption increased by 250 to 300 percent during the pandemic . <p> The next month was Earth Month . So , she made a simple commitment : pick up one bag of garbage a day in April to show her " love and gratitude to this beautiful lake Huron @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> The one-month pledge never ended . <p> Nearly five years later , she has collected more than 1,300 bags of garbage ( as of February 19 ) from the shores of Lake Huron with no plans to stop anytime soon . <p> " I can not stop now . It 's meditative ... I 'm cleaning up the beach but I 'm also cleaning the rubbish out of my head , " Lynn said . <p> " Despite the frustration of finding garbage every time , being at the lake for extended periods of time is a privilege and a joy . " <p> Even through snowy , crisp winters , she longs for the spring and summer months when she spends four or more times a week collecting trash . Each outing often stretched to three hours or more , especially after a busy summer day when picnickers have left the beach . <p> " I ca n't leave , " she laughed . <p> " I tell myself , ' just to that next tree ' and before I know it , hours have passed . " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ life , has turned her collections into educational tools , taking items to schools and community events to teach children about environmental responsibility . Climate change and heavy urbanization add another layer of stress on the freshwater system that supports over 40 million people and countless ecosystems . <p> The Great Lakes experienced historically low ice cover during the 2023-2024 winter , with Total Accumulated Ice Coverage ( TAC ) reaching just 2.5 percent , the lowest on record since the 1970s , as per data gathered by the Canadian Ice Service . <p> Lakes Superior , Michigan and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Ontario also saw ice far below historical averages . <p> The season was delayed by persistently warmer-than-normal temperatures , with ice forming more than a month later than usual and melting weeks earlier , leaving the lakes nearly ice-free by late March . <p> The following winter ( 2024-2025 ) conditions improved a bit with slightly higher ice coverage , though still below average for most of the season . Cold snaps in late January and February temporarily boosted ice , particularly on shallower lakes like Erie and St. Clair , where ice coverage briefly exceeded 90 percent . <p> But by early April , the Great Lakes were largely ice-free because of consecutive warm winters and shifting seasonal patterns . <p> In the latest binational State of the Great Lakes report , Canadian and American scientists sounded the alarm that although the Great Lakes remain in overall fair condition , shifting physical factors like warming waters , declining ice cover and changing precipitation patterns are affecting nutrient movement and habitat quality . <p> They make the case for ongoing basin-wide monitoring and assessment essential to protecting and restoring the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cuts and layoffs on both sides of the border . <p> Scientists found that warming air and water temperatures are altering seasonal cycles that historically regulated ecological stability . <p> It has extended the length of summer stratification , the period when warm surface water separates from colder deep water , which in turn , reduces vertical mixing , limiting the transfer of oxygen and nutrients between layers of the lake . <p> The result is a growing imbalance : offshore waters experience declining productivity while nearshore regions become increasingly vulnerable to nutrient overload . <p> This filtration creates unusually clear water , once considered a sign of improvement , but is now viewed as evidence of ecosystem disruption . Energy that once circulated through open-water food webs is redirected to bottom-dwelling species , contributing to declines in prey fish such as alewife and affecting predator species including salmon and lake trout . <p> Although new invasive species are entering the lakes less frequently than in previous decades , the report stresses that existing invaders continue to reshape ecosystems long after their arrival , making recovery complex and slow . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ even after management actions are introduced . <p> Historically , nutrient pollution dominated environmental discussions around the Great Lakes . Today , scientists observe a dual challenge : too many nutrients in some regions and too few in others . <p> In offshore zones , particularly in Lakes Huron and Michigan , invasive mussels remove phosphorus and plankton faster than natural processes can replenish them . This reduces biological productivity and may limit the growth and survival of fish species dependent on plankton-based food chains . Researchers warn that declining offshore productivity could have cascading impacts on commercial and recreational fisheries if trends continue . <p> At the same time , declining ice cover alters circulation patterns that once redistributed nutrients throughout the water column , reinforcing the imbalance between deep and shallow ecosystems . <p> But nearshore waters tell a different tale . <p> Harmful algal blooms , particularly in Lake Erie , were identified as one of the most visible consequences of climate change interacting with urbanization and agriculture . <p> More intense rainfall events wash fertilizers , manure and urban stormwater into tributaries that empty into the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ producing toxins harmful to humans , pets and wildlife . Scientists emphasize that bloom severity now depends not only on nutrient levels but also on warmer temperatures and shifting precipitation patterns that favour rapid algae growth . <p> Warmer water accelerates bloom development and prolongs bloom seasons , increasing risks to drinking water systems and coastal economies . <p> " We all need food . We all need places to live , " Steven Cooke , the new Commissioner for the Great Lakes Fishery Commission , told The Pointer . <p> " The key is doing these things differently ... letting nature do what it does well , filtering nutrients through wetlands , protecting riparian areas and designing stormwater systems that function more like ecosystems rather than just drains . " <p> In Ontario , Conservation Authorities ( CA ) that were created nearly eight decades ago to address these interconnected land-and-water challenges have been on the chopping block consistently in the eight years under the Progressive Conservative government . <p> In October last year , Premier Doug Ford 's government proposed consolidating Ontario 's 36 Conservation Authorities into seven @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ( OPCA ) . <p> Lynn worries about what such restructuring could mean for local environmental protection , particularly when paired with the expanded provincial powers introduced through Bill 5 . <p> " No one 's developing Greenbelt . @@134986312 <h> Sponsored Content <h> Sponsored Content <h> Canada 's Wildlife Is Sounding the Alarm . We Still Have Time to Act . <h> Sponsored Content By Wilder Institute <h> The evidence is clear . The solutions exist . What happens next is a choice . <h> Canada 's Wildlife Is in Decline <p> Canada is often defined by nature . From the Atlantic coastline to the boreal forest , from prairie grasslands to Pacific rainforests , our landscapes and wildlife are woven into our national identity . They are why people travel here , why communities thrive , and why many of us feel a deep sense of belonging to our country . <p> But beneath those postcard views , something is quietly going wrong . <p> The findings in the World Wildlife Fund Canada 's Living Planet Report Canada 2025 are stark . Wildlife populations across the country are declining at the fastest average rate recorded since reporting began nearly two decades ago . Animals , plants , and fungi are disappearing at a pace that should concern every Canadian . <h> Nature Is More Than Scenery <p> When @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ We depend on nature in fundamental ways . Globally , billions rely on wood for energy , and nature-inspired compounds for natural medicines and life-saving drugs . About 75 per cent of crops rely on pollinators to produce the foods many of us take for granted . As species decline , these systems weaken , putting our food security at risk . The health of our natural world is inseparable from the health of our communities . <h> The Limits of Protection Alone <p> On paper , Canada seems well-positioned to succeed . We are second in the world for remaining wilderness . We have protected areas , conservation laws , and a national commitment to halt biodiversity loss by 2030 . And yet , more than one in five species in Canada is now at some level of risk of extinction . <p> Much of Canadian conservation has focused on protecting land and water , which is essential . But with more than 80,000 species and one in five at risk , habitat protection alone is no longer enough . <p> Across the country , scientists have identified more @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ prevent extinction . These species face challenges such as extremely small or fragmented populations , or historic declines that have pushed them beyond the point where nature can recover without help . Without targeted intervention , some could disappear within a single generation . <h> Empty Forests and Silent Extinctions <p> Species are being pushed to the brink , or past it , by habitat fragmentation , unsustainable harvesting , climate change , and other pressures . The landscape may look intact , but the life within it has been hollowed out , a phenomenon known as ' empty forest syndrome ' . <p> It is a silent loss , easy to miss until it is too late . <h> Proof That Recovery Works <p> Canada has proven that species-focused recovery works . The Vancouver Island marmot , found nowhere else on Earth , fell to fewer than 30 individuals in the wild by 2003 . Today , thanks to coordinated conservation breeding , reintroduction , and long-term collaboration , the wild population has grown to approximately 427 marmots across 37 colonies . Once nearly silenced , their high-pitched whistles @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ what is possible when we decide extinction is not an option . <p> Success like this is not an accident . It required deliberate decisions to intervene directly on behalf of species at risk and the leadership to coordinate actions at scale . <h> The Wilder Canada Action Plan <p> The lessons learned from the Vancouver Island marmot and other species can be applied nationally . Species such as the Atlantic Whitefish , endemic to Nova Scotia , have populations too small or fragmented to recover without targeted action . Some already have limited recovery programs , but what they need most now is coordinated , collaborative , and sustained action . <p> This is the thinking behind the Wilder Canada Action Plan , an ambitious national-scale approach to species recovery led by the Wilder Institute . The plan builds on decades of conservation science and practical experience to support actions such as conservation translocations -- the careful movement of plants and animals to rebuild wild populations . This is about giving species a second chance to thrive where they belong . <p> For more than 270 species requiring active @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ implemented with the leadership of Indigenous nations , local communities , NGOs , and other partners . Success will be measured by the number of species benefiting from translocations and by slowing or stopping population decline . Over the next decade , 30 to 60 species currently receiving little or no recovery support will be directly assisted . <h> People at the Heart of Conservation <p> Conservation can not succeed if it rests solely on governments or a handful of organizations . Sustainable progress requires community partnerships , Indigenous leadership , knowledge sharing , and the empowerment of everyday people , as well as government action , to engage in conservation across Canada . <p> The Wilder Canada Action Plan will enable communities to act by providing training , sharing expertise , and mentoring partners to co-develop recovery programs . Together , these sustainable , collaborative actions are making a tangible difference . <h> A Call to Action for Canada <p> Canada has committed , through its 2030 Nature Strategy and global agreements like the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework , to halt species extinction and reduce biodiversity loss . Meeting @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ risk . Not more delay . Action . <p> The choice before us is clear . We can stay on our current path and accept a quieter , emptier future . Or we can decide that the wildlife that has shaped this country is worth fighting for . <p> Protecting nature is not a luxury . It is an investment in our shared future , our economy , our identity , and our responsibility to generations yet to come .

@@134997520 <p> For decades , northern Ontario residents have feared driving on their local stretches of the Trans-Canada Highway , the hazard-filled lifeline that connects their communities . <p> And for decades , their requests for the provincial and federal governments to fund upgrades have been ( mostly ) ignored . But Ottawa 's new spending commitments for defence-related infrastructure could be the key to making much needed improvements on these roads -- an essential link for this country . <p> Highway 11 and Highway 17 -- both parts of the Trans-Canada Highway system -- are the only east-west road links connecting the country through northern Ontario . The 1,000 kilometre section of Highway 11 that runs between North Bay and Nipigon is mostly two lanes , and long stretches of both roads have no passing lanes , medians or roadside stops . <p> Add heavy truck traffic and frequent winter storms to the mix , and the results are deadly . Already this year , nine people have died in collisions on Highway 11 and Highway 17 . In a recent tragedy in February , three family members were killed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ an SUV and a commercial vehicle . <p> Frequent closings wreak havoc on local communities . Highway 11 has 30 to 40 days of closure a year due to weather and collisions , and shutdowns are becoming more frequent as rapid freezing and thawing due to climate change has made winter salting and sanding less effective . <p> When the highways close , people ca n't get to work or home , children ca n't go to school , businesses ca n't meet customers or make deliveries , and medical appointments and emergency vehicles are disrupted . In choke points such as Nipigon , road closings cause lineups of trucks that jam the township , blocking residents from getting out of their driveways and creating risks for local drivers and pedestrians . <p> The impacts are n't only local . The highway closings cut the country in half , and the 8,400 commercial trucks that pass both routes each day ( including $200-million of goods travelling on Highway 11 ) are either delayed or detour through the U.S. <p> We need a dependable route across Canada that does n't run @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ can be used to cross much of northern Ontario , the roads converge into a single 120-kilometre stretch between Nipigon and Thunder Bay . When that stretch is closed , the only alternative is to drive through the U.S. This corridor , in particular , needs to be improved so goods , troops and military equipment can reliably pass through . <p> America 's interstate highways were championed by president Dwight D. Eisenhower , who saw the value of efficient highways for military and civilian use during the Cold War . Prime Minister Mark Carney 's pledge to spend 1.5 per cent of GDP annually on defence-related infrastructure , in addition to 3.5 per cent on core military needs , gives the federal government an additional impetus to set this project in motion . <p> Ontario Premier Doug Ford , a vocal proponent of drivers , should put his focus on this project , rather than on fantasies of a tunnel under the Highway 401 . This model would widen the highways to three lanes , with a centre passing lane that changes direction every two to five kilometres . The design has reduced head-on collisions , and it 's much cheaper than expanding roads to four lanes . In 2022 , the Ontario government committed to a pilot of 2+1 lanes on Highway 11 near North Bay , but the project has yet to break ground . <p> Local politicians are calling for better coordination between the transportation ministry and the Ontario Provincial Police during highway closings , dedicated truck waiting areas , and more roadside amenities . Management believes that these non-IFRS measures provide useful information to investors in measuring the financial performance of Canada Packers for the reasons outlined below . These measures do not have a standardized meaning prescribed by IFRS and therefore they may not be comparable to similarly titled measures presented by other publicly-traded companies and should not be construed as an alternative to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Adjusted Operating Earnings , Adjusted EBITDA , Adjusted EBITDA Margin , and Adjusted EBT are non-IFRS measures used by management to evaluate financial operating results . Adjusted Operating Earnings is defined as earnings before income taxes adjusted for items that are not considered representative of ongoing operational activities of the business and items where the economic impact of the transactions will be reflected in earnings in future periods when the underlying asset is sold or transferred . Adjusted EBITDA is defined as Adjusted Operating Earnings plus depreciation and amortization , adjusted for items included in other expense that are considered representative of ongoing operational activities of the business . Adjusted EBITDA Margin is calculated as Adjusted EBITDA divided by sales . Adjusted EBT is used annually by Canada Packers to evaluate its performance and is a component of calculating bonus entitlements under the Company 's short term incentive plan . It is defined as Adjusted EBITDA less depreciation and amortization and interest expense and income . Earnings Margin is calculated as earnings determined in accordance with IFRS , divided by sales . <p> The table below provides a reconciliation of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Consolidated Financial Statements to Adjusted Operating Earnings , Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted EBT for the periods ended as indicated below . @@134998329 <p> WINNIPEG -- WEATHER -- On March 4 , 1966 , Winnipeg and much of southern Manitoba were swallowed by a full-on prairie blizzard -- the kind that turns familiar streets into featureless white corridors and makes a short commute feel like a survival situation . It was n't " just a snowstorm . " By the next day 's reporting , the Winnipeg Free Press described a 14-hour blizzard that brought Greater Winnipeg " to a standstill , " with about 14 inches of snow whipped into deep drifts by winds up to 70 mph ( about 113 km/h ) . <p> Even decades later , the storm still works as a benchmark for how quickly a modern city can lose mobility , communications , and normal routines when visibility collapses and wind-driven snow starts piling up faster than crews can clear it . <p> Editor 's Note : This storm was memorable to me as a young child , I was amazed at the volume of snow . All the dads in the neighbourhood worked together to dig out the driveways . Clearing the snow took days . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 7 to 8 feet high . <p> Winnipeg Blizzard 1966 <h> What makes a blizzard different from " a lot of snow " <p> In Canada , blizzard warnings are tied more to visibility and wind than snowfall totals . Environment and Climate Change Canada describes blizzard conditions as high winds causing widespread reductions in visibility ( around 400 metres or less ) due to falling and/or blowing snow . <p> That matters because it explains why cities can be paralyzed even when snowfall totals do n't sound extreme at first glance : once the wind starts moving snow around , roads disappear and plows ca n't keep ahead of drifting . <h> The storm 's setup : a classic " Colorado Low " <p> Many of the most punishing Prairie blizzards trace back to a Colorado Low -- a powerful low-pressure system that forms in the U.S. Rockies/High Plains region and then tracks northeast . <p> The Transcona Museum notes the March 4 , 1966 storm was driven by a Colorado low and hit Winnipeg-area communities with about 35 cm of snow and gusts around 110 km/h , closing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the border , NOAA 's National Weather Service documented the broader March 2 -- 5 , 1966 blizzard across the Northern Plains as a long-duration event fueled by an intense Colorado Low -- producing heavy snow and very strong winds over a wide region . <p> Winnipeg was in the sweet spot when that system delivered its worst punch to southern Manitoba . <h> How the shutdown unfolded in Winnipeg <p> From the Free Press coverage the next day , you can see the sequence that 's familiar to anyone who has lived through a major city blizzard : <p> 1 ) Overnight snow becomes morning chaos.Snow began after midnight , but the real danger rose with the wind : snow was whipped into high drifts , and by Friday , activity across the city stalled . <p> 2 ) Transit becomes the first domino.Buses were blocked by drifts , and getting them moved became part of the initial dig-out effort . In a city that relies on public transit for thousands of workers , once buses stop , everything from staffing hospitals to stocking stores becomes harder . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reported about 1,600 people sought refuge at Winnipeg 's two largest retail stores -- Eaton 's and The Bay -- as the storm cut off normal travel . <p> 4 ) Emergency response shifts from " service " to " improvisation . " The Free Press described police constables acting as midwives when travel to hospital was " impossible , " underscoring how fast routine emergencies become high-stakes when roads are impassable . <p> 5 ) Communications become the lifeline.One striking detail : a radio call to Mayor Stephen Juba helped trigger an organized response -- an emergency centre and bulletins to news outlets -- because the scale of the blizzard was n't immediately obvious at the start of the day . <h> The human and economic toll <p> Historic storms are remembered for snowbanks and dramatic photos , but their real impact shows up in the difficult , personal outcomes : <p> The Free Press front page noted two men died " at blizzard 's height . " <p> Cleanup , overtime , damaged vehicles , stranded commuters , and interrupted business operations all translate to costs that can @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ wind-driven drifting makes clearing slow and repetitive . <p> And the disruption does n't end when snow stops falling . The " after storm " period is when cities face their second crisis : digging out while keeping hospitals , fire protection , and essential supply lines functioning . <h> Why blizzards hit major cities so hard <p> Big cities have advantages -- more equipment , more staffing , more infrastructure -- but they also have built-in vulnerabilities : <h> Transportation gridlock spreads fast <p> A few stuck buses or jackknifed vehicles can cascade into system-wide congestion , blocking plows and emergency vehicles . When visibility drops , even experienced drivers make mistakes , and the margin for error disappears . <h> Cities depend on constant staffing <p> Hospitals , utilities , airports , transit control centres , and communications systems all run on shifts . If workers ca n't get in -- or ca n't get home -- fatigue becomes its own hazard . <h> Supply chains are " just in time " <p> Grocery stores , pharmacies , and fuel distribution depend on frequent deliveries . A single @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ if the storm covers a wide region . <h> Power and communications are exposed <p> High winds , drifting , and ice can damage lines and hamper repair crews . Even when power holds , customer support and emergency call systems can be overwhelmed . <h> The lasting lesson of March 4 , 1966 <p> Winnipeg 's 1966 blizzard was n't only memorable because of the snow totals -- it 's remembered because it showed how a city can be functionally cut off in hours when wind , visibility , and drifting line up . <p> The practical takeaway for any major city is simple : the " best " blizzard response is n't heroic digging -- it 's reducing exposure before the worst conditions arrive : <p> keep traffic off key corridors early , <p> open warming/shelter spaces quickly ( downtown , transit hubs ) , <p> prioritize emergency routes and hospitals , <p> communicate clearly and repeatedly through radio , mobile alerts , and social channels . <p> Because when the wind-driven snow starts piling into walls and the street grid disappears , the city does n't need @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ might be understated . <p> NetNewsledger.com or NNL offers news , information , opinions and positive ideas for Thunder Bay , Ontario , Northwestern Ontario and the world . @@135032679 <p> Leaders in Canada 's nascent carbon-removal industry have joined with several corporate and financial backers as well as the federal government in a bid to attract $100-million in project investments by 2030 . <p> The effort , called the Advance Carbon Removal Coalition , seeks to position the country as a top global player in such technologies as direct air capture , biomass carbon removal and direct ocean capture -- all designed to extract carbon dioxide , or CO2 , from the atmosphere for storage deep underground . <p> The organizers aim to help establish networks to draw capital from a range of domestic and international investors for projects across the country , and increase demand for credible carbon credits . <p> The group is slated to announce the coalition 's formationat an Ottawa conference on Thursday hosted by Carbon Removal Canada , a non-profit group that is leading it . <p> The financial and corporate partners include Bank of Montreal BMO-T , Royal Bank of Canada RY-T , ClimeFi , NorthX NIX-CN , Shopify Inc . SHOP-T and Vancity , which , along with Ottawa , have collectively @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> " I make the rounds , including internationally , and when it comes to carbon removal , Canada 's hot , " Ed Whittingham , Advance Carbon Removal 's founding director , said in an interview . <p> " That 's a great thing . We 've got the right trades who can build these projects , we 've got sophisticated finance and capital markets , we 've got companies that understand the tech , we 've got coastlines and biomass , suitable geology . All those boxes that need to be checked are pretty much checked . " <p> Meanwhile , the federal government has designed a regulatory and policy framework to support the development of projects , including industrial carbon pricing and investment tax credits , said Mr. Whittingham , an Alberta-based veteran of Canadian environmental and economic initiatives . <p> Carbon dioxide removal , or CDR , differs from carbon capture and storage , as it extracts the greenhouse gas from the ambient air rather than from point sources such as industrial smokestacks . <p> Its proponents see it as one of several ways to help @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ energy . The global CDR market could be worth as much as US$1.2-trillion by 2050 , McKinsey &amp; Co. has estimated . <p> The coalition organizers take some cues from the Business Renewables Centre-Canada , an initiative of the Pembina Institute that , since its formation in 2019 , has helped boost wind and solar development by providing connections for corporate buyers of power purchase agreements . Like that organization , it will not act as an investor itself , but provide a platform . <p> The targeted level of CDR investment is expected to support an industry that employs a wide range of technologies in locations across the country , and attracts sizable sums of foreign capital for projects , Mr. Whittingham said . <p> Already , some investments that had been planned for the United States have relocated to Canada as a result of U.S. President Donald Trump 's cancellation of green incentive programs last year . <p> Today , 78 CDR companies operate in Canada and 48 projects are under way or planned , according to Carbon Removal Canada . Most are small in scale , with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ projects would account for 10.9 million tonnes annually , equal to the emissions from 2.4 million gas-powered cars . <p> The coalition 's corporate and financial members have experience moving money into the CDR industry , co-ordinator David Hochhalter said . That includes credit purchases , off-take deals , equity investments and project financing . <p> The group will concentrate on helping to bring in investment , rather than debating the process 's environmental benefits , he said . <p> Critics of CDR contend the technology could be used as a cover for increasing fossil-fuel use , and that it can only be effective at a massive scale . <p> " We 're looking at the importance of financial agreements and financial risk-taking in this space , in order to scale , elevate and bring that understanding -- advance the technology so that it is something that is reliable and takes care of some of that skepticism , " Mr. Hochhalter said . <p> Federal Minister of Environment and Climate Change Julie Dabrusin said in a statement that CDR is key to Canada meeting its net-zero goals , and that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ supporting the development of projects . <p> Editor 's note : This article has been updated to state that the federal government , along with financial and corporate partners , have collectively contributed $75-million in financing to the carbon-removal industry to date .

The Technology Networks editorial team 4 FOOD &amp; BEVERAGE ANALYSIS Challenges and Solutions in Food Fraud Testing Nicholas Philip Gaunt , PhD A multi-billion pounds criminal enterprise lurks amid our supermarket shelves - food crimes , including adulteration and fraud . Not only are these crimes impacting our wallets , they are a serious threat to public health . They include activities such as mislabeling , replacing a food or ingredient with another inferior substance and even poisoning . This is a global concern because of how food crime is evolving . The complexity of food supply chains , the globalization of food markets and a lack of transparency heighten the vulnerability of the food sector . So , rethinking how we combat food crime by using technology is imperative . Serious fraud and related criminality in food supply chains , or " food crimes " , now inflict an estimated $40 billion in yearly global damages . Products such as virgin olive oil , manuka honey , wine and vast amounts of seafood top the most commonly adulterated foods . As occurrences of food fraud become more prevalent , food manufacturers , processors and retailers are intensifying their efforts to combat this issue . Challenges in food authenticity testing One of the foremost challenges in ensuring food authenticity is the sheer variety and complexity of fraudulent practices . The methods used to deceive can range from simple mislabeling to sophisticated adulteration involving multiple ingredients . This diversity makes it difficult to have a one-size-fits-all approach to testing . Credit : iStock/AnnaStills TECHNOLOGYNETWORKS.COM FOOD &amp; BEVERAGE ANALYSIS 5 The global nature of the food supply chain further complicates matters . With ingredients often sourced from different parts of the world , the complexity of verifying their authenticity increases . A single product may pass through numerous hands before reaching the consumer , each step presenting an opportunity for fraud . " As our food supply chains grow more complex and global , ensuring the authenticity and safety of what we eat becomes more critical , " explains Dr. Patrick Sears , a senior lecturer of chemistry and forensic analysis at the University of Surrey . " Rapid , reliable testing methods that can detect contaminants and verify authenticity are no longer just a luxury -- they 're essential for protecting consumers across borders . " Advancements in analytical technologies Fortunately , advancements in technology have significantly impacted the field of food authenticity testing . Analytical technologies such as gas or liquid chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry ( GC-MS and LC-MS ) , and nuclear magnetic resonance ( NMR ) spectroscopy have emerged as vital tools in the detection of food fraud . " As food supply chains become more globalized , there 's a greater need for advanced analytical tools to ensure authenticity , " says Dr. Sears . " Technologies like NMR and mass spectrometry allow us not only to detect fraud but also to trace the geographical origin of products , crucial in protecting both consumers and producers . " GC-MS , LC-MS , NMR -- these are all familiar instruments for an analytical scientist , and they have come on a long way in a relatively short amount of time . Dr. Sears spoke to Technology Networks about what innovation with a conventional instrument looks like . " Two of the breakthroughs we 're looking for in food authenticity testing are speed and ease of use . In the fast-paced world of food production we need answers now , not weeks later . The ability to stop a contaminated batch before it leaves the manufacturing site is critical . " " Modern analytical technologies have become more user-friendly , allowing even non-scientists to operate them effectively , " he adds . " This democratization of technology is crucial for enhancing food safety and authenticity testing . " Olive oil in particular is a very high-value product , which makes it more vulnerable to fraud . Adulteration of olive oil , such as blending with cheaper oils or mislabeling lower-quality products as premium , is common in the olive oil industry . Advanced analytical techniques like NMR spectroscopy and high-resolution mass spectroscopy are critical for detecting these types of fraud . These methods provide detailed molecular insights , enabling scientists to distinguish genuine olive oil from adulterated or counterfeit products . " Some products , like olive oil and manuka honey , present these rather unique challenges , " notes Dr. Sears . " The fact that more manuka honey is sold in the UK than produced globally shows how critical food authenticity testing is to maintain trust and safety in the industry . " Mass spectrometry can be used without chromatography to help verify the authenticity of ingredients , and can be particularly useful for distinguishing between genuine and counterfeit oils and ensuring that the correct meat is in your frozen lasagna . To enhance the effectiveness of these analytical technologies , there are also several methods and complementary techniques such as principal component analysis ( PCA ) and partial least squares discriminant analysis ( PLS-DA ) that are employed . A combination of statistical methods and automated approaches helps interpret the complex data generated by analytical techniques and identify patterns indicative of fraud . " The goal is to take what is traditionally high-end technology , requiring a PhD-level scientist , and make it accessible for food scientists in authenticity labs , " Dr. Sears explains . " This way , you do n't need a mass spectrometry expert -- you just need a tool that can provide a simple yes or no . " TECHNOLOGYNETWORKS.COM FOOD &amp; BEVERAGE ANALYSIS 6 Regulatory frameworks and their limitations While regulations provide a framework for preventing food fraud , the pace at which fraudsters adapt means that legislation can struggle to keep up . This necessitates ongoing updates and improvements in regulatory measures . In some cases , regulations are not uniformly enforced , creating gaps in the system . For example , smaller producers or those operating outside of mainstream markets might not be subject to the same level of scrutiny , leaving opportunities for fraud . " Preventing food adulteration requires constant vigilance , " says Dr. Dana Watson , professor of food management and techniques at the National University of La Matanza . " Regulations need to evolve continuously , staying ahead of emerging threats , but the reality is that fraudsters often move faster than the legislation can adapt . Unfortunately , the process of updating these guidelines frequently lags behind , leaving gaps that can be exploited . " In some cases , regulations are not uniformly enforced , which can create gaps in the system . For example , smaller producers or those operating outside of mainstream markets might not be subject to the same level of scrutiny , leaving opportunities for fraud . The global supply chain dilemma The international nature of today 's food supply chain introduces additional complexity to authenticity testing . Ingredients often travel through multiple countries and various processing stages before reaching the final product . This extensive journey can obscure the origins and integrity of the food . The global supply chain means that reliance on a network of suppliers , each with their own standards and practices , is necessary . Ensuring authenticity requires robust verification processes at every stage , which can be challenging to implement consistently . Even with advanced tracking systems , risks associated with third-party suppliers and the potential for fraudulent documentation remain . Consumer awareness and protection While much of the focus is on industry and regulatory measures , consumers also have a role to play in protecting themselves from food fraud . Educating consumers on how to identify and avoid potentially fraudulent products can complement industry efforts and help reduce the impact of food fraud . " Consumer education is crucial . It 's difficult to detect food adulteration unless it causes symptoms , and many issues go unreported. " says Dr. Watson , reiterating that consumer vigilance is a key part of the solution . Simple practices , such as checking labels , purchasing from reputable sources and being aware of product origins , can help mitigate the risks of encountering fraudulent products . Transparency from brands and clear , informative labeling can empower consumers to make more informed choices . It is also important for consumers to be aware of the signs of potential fraud , such as unusual pricing or inconsistencies in product quality . " Public outrage often stems from confusion over mislabeled products , even when the alternatives are legal , " Dr. Watson explains . " For example , products like grated cheese or yogurt alternatives may clearly state modifications on the packaging , but similar names can lead to misunderstandings and media uproar . " Shaping a transparent future The fight against food fraud is ongoing , and while significant strides have been made in technology and regulation , challenges remain . The global supply chain , evolving fraudulent techniques and the need for continuous improvement in regulations highlight the complexities of ensuring food authenticity . However , with advancements in testing technologies , a collaborative approach involving industry stakeholders , TECHNOLOGYNETWORKS.COM FOOD &amp; BEVERAGE ANALYSIS 7 regulatory bodies and informed consumers , the battle against food fraud continues to progress . As Dr. Patrick Sears and Dr. Dana Watson have illustrated , tackling the mammoth issue of food fraud requires a variety of tools and a multifaceted strategy that embraces technological innovation and robust regulations . " For greater transparency , control , dynamic legislation and consumer education must come together to combat food fraud effectively , " says Dr. Watson . And , by addressing these challenges head-on , the food industry can work towards a more trustworthy food supply chain , ultimately safeguarding consumer wellbeing and maintaining the integrity of the food we eat . His research expertise and background include developing analytical chemistry solutions for complex problems and understanding how analytical systems can be broken down to improve precision and accuracy . 8 FOOD &amp; BEVERAGE ANALYSIS The Science of Flow in Food Testing Abbey Thiel , PhD Rheological analysis has become an indispensable tool for the food industry , helping to increase manufacturing efficiency , reduce product failures and ensure consistent textures that consumers trust . Rheology refers to how materials , including foods , will deform and flow when stress or shear is applied.1 At its core , rheological tests quantify mechanical properties such as viscosity , yield stress and elasticity . Modern rheometers extend far beyond these basics -- probing structural responses like recovery , phase transitions between liquid and solid states and network formations . Dr. Dieyckson Freire , a researcher at the University of Wisconsin -- Madison who studies frozen desserts , highlights this in his work , " Rheology gives us insight into the architecture of foods . In ice cream , it can link meltdown behavior and sensory characteristics directly to the product 's structural and compositional factors . " Rheology stands out among analytical methods because few techniques have such wide-ranging implications . For example , it can guide factory design while also revealing how consumers will experience the final product . Even a basic grasp of its principles reveals why rheology is such a powerful bridge connecting science , industry and the eating experience . What is rheology ? To gain meaningful results from any rheological test , it 's critical to first understand which property of the food should be evaluated . As rheometers are capable of such a wide array of measurements , selecting the appropriate one requires careful consideration . Credit : iStock/kirinphoto TECHNOLOGYNETWORKS.COM FOOD &amp; BEVERAGE ANALYSIS 9 Testing the viscosity of a food , for example , is one of the most common measurements performed on a rheometer . Viscosity refers to the resistance of a material to flow.2 While traditional viscometers -- arguably the predecessor to modern rheometers -- can also measure viscosity , they lack the broader capabilities of rheometers . From a microscopic standpoint , viscosity arises in food due to the different molecules present . This variation in shape and size creates internal friction once the sample is put into motion by a viscometer or rheometer . In practical terms , viscosity determines whether a food pours easily , feels thick or thin , or clings to a surface . For example , salad dressings , sauces and ketchup all rely on viscosity to deliver the right mouthfeel but also to perform as expected -- like a dipping sauce coating a chicken nugget or a marinade adhering evenly to meat . Beyond viscosity , ketchup also demonstrates another critical parameter that can be measured : yield stress , which is the amount of force needed to get a material to begin flowing.3 If you 've ever shaken a ketchup bottle and nothing came out , it 's because you had n't yet applied enough force to overcome the yield stress . Yield stress values are critical , not only for how consumers interact with the final product , but also for its processing and packaging . Stress values determine how a product will behave during steps such as pumping , extrusion or storage . " Understanding yield stress is key to predicting how ice cream will hold its structure during storage , transport or when it finally reaches the consumer , " Freire noted . A more intensive approach is to quantify the liquid-like properties as the viscous modulus ( G ' ' ) and the solidlike properties as the elastic modulus ( G ' ) . The ratio of these two values , called tan d ( or the loss tangent ) , quickly indicates whether a sample behaves more like a liquid ( tan d &gt; 1 ) or more like a solid ( tan d &lt; 1 ) . The benefit of determining the viscous and elastic modulus of a sample is that it gives a more detailed look into the microstructure of a food . As Dr. Etske Bijl , an associate professor at Wageningen University and Research , explained , " By measuring G ' and G " , we can see how the protein and fat network in cheese responds to stress . These values reveal whether the structure is soft , firm , flexible or stiff . " With an understanding of what properties of a sample should be tested , the next challenge is to select the appropriate technique and testing conditions to glean the most useful insights and information . Rheological techniques and tests Rheometers are powerful instruments capable of running a wide variety of tests . Understanding which one to apply to your sample is critical to obtaining meaningful results . To generate relevant data , tests should be conducted under conditions that mimic how the food will be processed , stored or consumed . One of the most fundamental rheological tests is generating a flow curve . This is critical because viscosity is not a fixed value , but changes with variations in conditions such as shear rate or temperature . The shape of a flow curve reveals whether a food behaves as a Newtonian fluid , like water with constant viscosity , or as a non-Newtonian fluid , like ketchup , where viscosity changes with applied shear . Freire highlighted the utility of this approach , saying , " Flow curves are especially valuable in dairy systems such as ice cream mixes , because they capture viscosity and predict how the mix will behave during processing . This insight helps optimize structural stability and ensures smooth production . " While flow curves describe how a food behaves under steady shear , oscillatory tests probe its structure under small , repeated deformations . By applying a gentle oscillating stress or strain , this type of test will measure both the G ' and G " of a sample . TECHNOLOGYNETWORKS.COM FOOD &amp; BEVERAGE ANALYSIS 10 As many foods are gels , emulsions or dispersions , oscillatory tests can elucidate how these different microstructures strengthen , break down or remain stable overtime . This type of test goes beyond viscosity alone to capture changes to a food 's structure that could occur during manufacturing , storage and consumption . Bijl , who applies oscillatory rheology to study cheese production , explains : " By tracking G ' during acid and rennet gelation , we can watch liquid milk transform into a gel and ultimately into cheese . We have seen that cow 's milk tends to develop stronger acid gels while goat milk often forms firmer rennet gels . " She added that " These differences highlight how oscillatory tests capture not only gel strength but also how processing conditions like heating reshape the microstructure of dairy systems . " Creep and recovery tests measure how a material deforms under constant stress , and whether deformation is reversible once the stress is removed . In practice , a steady load is applied to the sample to observe its creep , or time-dependent deformation . When the load is released , the recovery phase reveals the balance between reversible and permanent deformation . As Freire noted , " Creep and recovery tests are especially valuable in ice cream because they capture transient behavior and structural recovery . These measurements provide insight into the resilience of the ice cream matrix , helping us understand how the product responds to stress during handling and if it can recover its structure afterward . " Stress growth tests measure how a material responds when stress is gradually increased over time . Unlike creep and recovery , which evaluate deformation under a constant load , stress growth tests identify the point at which a material 's internal structure can no longer withstand the applied force . This critical threshold , known as the yield stress , reflects the moment when a food 's microstructure begins to flow or collapse . In practical terms , it helps predict processing behavior , such as whether a product can maintain stability during pumping or mixing . Temperature ramps and sweeps are used to evaluate how a food 's structure changes under controlled heating or cooling . By gradually varying the temperature while applying oscillatory stress , researchers can monitor transitions such as gelation , melting or protein denaturation . " Oscillatory thermo-rheometry can evaluate how the structure of ice cream melts under various temperature changes , " explained Freire . Practically speaking , temperature sweeps help predict how a product will hold up during storage , shipping and consumption , making them a critical tool for linking thermal conditions to texture and stability . Frequency sweeps are used to probe the timedependent behavior of foods by applying oscillatory stress at different frequencies . Unlike temperature sweeps , which reveal how a material responds to thermal changes , frequency sweeps examine how structure behaves over short versus long timescales . These measurements are especially powerful for foods with complex microstructures , such as gels , doughs or emulsions . For example , soft gels often show strong frequency dependence , behaving more like liquids at low frequencies and more like solids at higher ones . By contrast , strong gels typically remain solid-like across frequencies , reflecting the presence of stable , crosslinked networks . The future of food rheology Looking forward , novel approaches are pushing rheology into new territory . Interfacial rheology is emerging as a powerful way to study multiphasic systems such as foams , emulsions and dispersions , whereas thin interfacial layers often act as points of instability . Extensional rheology takes a different approach by examining how materials behave when stretched to reveal critical information about dough strength , extrusion behavior and fiber formation . Coupling TECHNOLOGYNETWORKS.COM FOOD &amp; BEVERAGE ANALYSIS 11 rheology with tribology is also opening new ways to study oral processing , lubrication and texture perception . Together , these innovations signal a future where rheological methods are a mainstay in testing food quality and a driver of innovation in how products are designed , processed and ultimately experienced . Dr. Freire also teaches Dairy Products Evaluation and coaches the UW -- Madison team for the Collegiate Dairy Products Evaluation Contest , combining education , industry collaboration , and scientific advancement . 12 FOOD &amp; BEVERAGE ANALYSIS Inside the AI App That Can Estimate Food Calories Leo Bear-McGuiness The past few years have seen a giant leap in artificial intelligence capabilities . Companies all over the world , in all different sectors , are now scrambling to find ways to incorporate the powerful new technology into their products and services . You might think , then , that any major food-AI advances would come courtesy of international food conglomerates , the kind that have vast resources and existing R&amp;D labs at their disposal . And yet , one of the more compelling recent AI-enabled advances relevant to the food industry has just emerged from academia -- from a research team that usually study firefighters and fire safety practices , no less . The prototype app developed by the team can reportedly estimate the calorie count of any piece of food or meal presented to a phone camera . To learn more about the AI methodology behind the app and its vast applications , Technology Networks spoke with its co-developer , Prabodh Panindre , a research associate professor at NYU Tandon School of Engineering . Q : Could you outline your research background ? A : I 've been working with the US fire service for almost 20 years now . There are fire departments who use the firefighting procedures developed through my research . One of the problems with the fire service is that 50% of firefighters die because of cardiac events . Most people think burns and smoking inhalation should be the major reason for firefighter deaths , but that 's not true ; cardiovascular disease is the major reason . And since I was working with the fire service , I wanted to address that issue . And we thought we could use AI . Credit : iStock/alvarez TECHNOLOGYNETWORKS.COM FOOD &amp; BEVERAGE ANALYSIS 13 We have actually developed several technologies using AI . We have a technology to detect fire and smoke through live video streaming ; we have a technology for detecting heart conditions like arrhythmia . Next , we wanted to address the obesity in the fire service . Firefighting is a very stressful job , but if you can allow the firefighters to take a picture and tell them whatever they are eating has this many calories -- ' these are the nutrients , these are the carbs , this is the fat , this is the protein ' -- maybe that can help them to make better decisions in terms of managing their diet , and that will help them , ultimately , to mitigate obesity . The original idea was to use AI to detect food objects and estimate the calories . It was developed for fire practice , but it is also applicable to the general population , because obesity is a major issue worldwide . Q : Could you talk a bit more about that methodology behind the app ? A : We tried to collect as many images as we could . We actually collected more than 100,000 , and we created a huge data set and manually annotated all those images , so the app can actually detect more than 200 food classes . There were a lot of images for pizza , whereas there were few images for , say , chicken curry . So , there was a possibility of bias . We basically implemented a logic to avoid those biases , and we tried to make a data set which was very balanced . The next challenge was , when you estimate the calories , you need to identify the volume of the different food objects . There are databases which are well established . There is a UK database and a US database , and they have the 100-gram calorie value . From that , we can actually estimate the calorie values of the entire food if we know the whole mass of the object . Let 's say it 's 1 kilo of chicken , and if you have 100 grams , then you can just multiply and get the whole value of the calories for the entire 1 kilo of chicken . The next challenge was basically to estimate the mass of the food object . You get that based on the density and the volume ; you can get the density values from the databases as well . We used a depth map to estimate the thickness . So , using those , we can actually estimate the volume of the full object , and with the density values from the databases , you can get the whole mass of the object . And then , from that , you can use the calorie values from the UK and the US databases and get the calorie value . Let 's say there 's a chicken burger . When you do the detection , you can not just identify it 's a burger , because the calorie values of burgers can vary greatly , depending on where you buy it from . What you have to detect is the different items in that burger . This is the bread , the size of the bread , the thickness of the bread , the chicken , the dimensions of the chicken , onion , everything . It 's called full segmentation . Now , there are a lot of calculations that happen in the background ; I 'll try to simplify it for you . You take a picture , it goes to the AI models , AI does all the calculation and then you get the values of the burger , the bread , the chicken and the other items . Q : How did you source the images of food that were less accounted for in the UK and US databases ? A : There are a lot of open-source databases . We utilized them . We did n't just want to focus on US food , we also wanted to see whether we can detect Indian food , Middle Eastern food , Chinese food , Korean food , etc . Sometimes we actually searched for those kinds of images and created our own data set . Q : What is an app user presented with when they scan a certain food ? Just the calorie estimate , or some other health information , for instance ? A : When it comes to the final result , a person uses the app , takes picture of a piece of food , and the algorithm gets the broad range of its calorific content . TECHNOLOGYNETWORKS.COM FOOD &amp; BEVERAGE ANALYSIS 14 In terms of calorie requirements , every consumer is different . A firefighter has a very busy day . Maybe they should consume more than 3,000 or 4,000 calories . While I 'm just always sitting on my chair , not so physically active , so my requirement is just 2,000 or 2,500 calories . So , if you take a picture , you will get the amount of calories in that particular food item , and if you keep taking the pictures throughout the day , at one point , it will tell you , " OK , you got enough . You do n't need to consume more calories . " It then gives you a suggestion , maybe slow down or drink water . One of the major problems in the fire service is dehydration . Q : What feedback have you had so far from the firefighters ? Have they found it useful ? A : Definitely . One of the problems in the fire service is that everybody has all these health trackers , but the user has to interpret their own data . Now , something is interpreting the data for the firefighters and giving them a suggestion . So the app can be very useful . There 's no question . And I 'm sure this methodology can be applicable to other emergency personnel and a wide variety of subsets of the population . Q : Where do you see the future for the app ? A : After I published that paper , it was picked up by a lot of news media , and other agencies approached us to do different types of projects . So , yes , we are working on different projects , trying to use the same technology for other types of populations . Perhaps it could even be used for restaurants , because a lot of restaurants do n't have the calorie information on their menu . Due to their hydrophobic nature , PFAS accumulate in fatty foods like oils , butter and processed meats . High consumption of pork , beef and hot dogs has been linked to higher PFAS levels in the blood . Fish and seafood are the most significant dietary source of PFAS . A diet rich in whole fruits , vegetables , grains and pasta is associated with lower PFAS levels , possibly because fiber helps remove PFAS from the body . Tea , especially unsweetened tea , is associated with higher PFAS levels -- likely due to contaminated tea bags or packaging . Tea Despite contamination in fresh produce , cooking at home is still the better option . Studies show that foods from fast-food restaurants -- especially hot dogs , burgers and fries -- are linked to higher PFAS levels , likely due to grease-resistant packaging . Click here to view the full infographic Is My Food Full of PFAS ? 16 FOOD &amp; BEVERAGE ANALYSIS Current Analytical Techniques in Food Science Srividya Kailasam , PhD The modernization of agriculture , development of sophisticated techniques for processing and storing foods and shipment of both food ingredients and processed foods around the globe have created a multibillion-dollar food industry . However , this growth has been accompanied by increasing concerns over food safety , authenticity and fraud . The availability of dietary supplements also presents opportunities as well as new challenges in terms of human health . Numerous regulations have been issued by governmental and non-governmental agencies to ensure food quality and safety ; and compliance with these typically rests on " food testing " using modern scientific techniques . A plethora of studies are carried out to examine various aspects such as : * Physical description * Chemical composition * Sensory assessment * Authenticity * Contamination In this listicle , we will explore some of the well-established aspects of and techniques used for food analysis . Credit : iStock/MilosCirkovic TECHNOLOGYNETWORKS.COM FOOD &amp; BEVERAGE ANALYSIS 17 Sample preparation As with any analysis , sample preparation plays an important part in ensuring selectivity and sensitivity in the results obtained . C ? mara et al have reviewed applications of many " green " extraction techniques such as quick , easy , cheap , effective , rugged and safe ( QuEChERS ) , solidphase microextraction ( SPME ) , microextraction in packed syringe ( MEPS ) and dispersive liquid -- liquid microextraction ( DLLME ) that are used to : a. improve extraction efficiency b. optimize the use of resources c. minimize the generation of environmental contaminants These sample preparation techniques are used to extract and pre-concentrate a variety of organic and inorganic analytes such as pesticides and trace metals in dairy products , beverages , spices and more.1 Spectroscopic techniques Analysis of raw materials , whole foods and processed food during production and distribution is crucial to ensure quality and safety . This necessitates online as well as onsite testing using field-portable instruments and kits . Spectroscopic techniques are the " go-to " methods for food testing due to their ease-of-use and cost-effectiveness . Miniaturization of near-infrared ( NIR ) spectroscopy instruments has facilitated testing of foods from farms to shelf . Bec et al have reviewed numerous applications for portable , miniaturized NIR instruments for detecting adulteration in milk , freshness of meat , food fraud in seafoods , quality of fruits and vegetables and the geographical origin of rice among others.2 In a review of applications of Raman spectroscopic methods , the authors have shown that this technique has been used to detect physical ( microplastic ) , chemical ( mycotoxins , pesticides , additives , adulterants , allergens , heavy metals and toxins ) , biological ( microbes and toxins ) , and environmental contaminants ( bisphenol A ) in foods such as meat , smoked salmon , ground maize , adulterated olive oil , adulterated honey , adulterated butter , fruits and white wine.3 Nuclear magnetic resonance ( NMR ) spectroscopy is not a commonly used technique for food analysis due to its limited sensitivity and dynamic range . Moreover , it requires trained operators and is a relatively expensive technique for routine analysis . Yet , the feasibility of analyses of complex samples without prior purification or separation makes NMR a valuable technique for food analysis . Hatzakis has reviewed several applications of NMR such as composition analysis , food authentication and quality control.4 Electrochemical methods Electrochemical methods offer sensitive , low-cost solutions for food analysis . Moreover , these methods often require minimal sample preparation and exhibit wide dynamic ranges for organic and inorganic analytes . Detection and quantification of contaminants and degradation products in milk using voltammetric and amperometric methods has been reviewed by Motshakeri et al . A variety of analytes such as adulterants ( melamine , urea and baking soda ) , allergens ( ? -lactoglobulin ) , antioxidants ( uric acid and ascorbic acid ) , endocrine disruptors ( bisphenol A , insecticides and pesticides ) and heavy metals have been measured in milk samples using these electrochemical methods.5 Electrochemical sensors provide rapid and accurate means to measure target analytes in different foodstuffs . For instance , electrochemical sensors have been used to measure lactose and L-lactic acid in yogurt , nitrite in sausage samples and hydrogen peroxide in different fruit juice samples.6 TECHNOLOGYNETWORKS.COM FOOD &amp; BEVERAGE ANALYSIS 18 Chromatographic methods Detection of nanogram and microgram quantities of analytes in complex food grains or food products may necessitate their separation prior to analysis . Chromatographic and electrophoretic techniques are used to evaluate the nutritional content , flavor profile , safety and several other parameters during the various stages of food production . Per- and polyfluorinated alkyl substances ( PFAS ) are a new class of chemical contaminants . Of the different PFAS , perfluorooctanesulfonic acid ( PFOS ) and perfluorooctanoic acid ( PFOA ) are ubiquitous in the environment and are known to cause cancer and several other diseases in humans . Iannone et al have reviewed numerous liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry ( LC-MS ) and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry ( GC-MS ) techniques for the analysis of PFAS in fruits and vegetables , milk and dairy products , eggs , seafood , meat , beverages and honey.7 Gas chromatography -- ion mobility spectrometry ( GC -- IMS ) is a highly sensitive technique that has been applied for the analysis of volatile compounds in food samples . These molecules impart characteristic aromas to foodstuffs and help in ascertaining the quality and freshness of the product as well as supporting food classification . For example , GC-IMS has been used to : * classify olive oils based on their geographical origin and types ( extra virgin or pomace or mixed with refined olive oil ) * detect adulteration of canola oil and palm oil * determine the freshness of fish products by measuring the increase in concentration of certain volatile amines * detect off-flavor ( unpleasant odors ) in wine caused by 2,4.6-trichloroanisole ( 2,4,6-TCA ) produced by fungal infection of the wine bottle cork These and numerous other applications have been carried out using GC-IMS , which is an important technique for food flavor analysis.8 Flavonoids are important functional components of foods with numerous health benefits such as antioxidant , antiviral , antibacterial , antidiabetic and anticancer activities . Liquid chromatographyquadrupole time-of-flight tandem mass spectrometry ( LC-Q-TOF-MS/MS ) enables separation , identification and quantification of flavonoids in complex food matrices . This technique has been applied for determining : * types and contents of flavonoids in agricultural products * changes in the structure and quantity of flavonoids during food processing * flavonoid metabolites in tissues and organs9 Capillary electrophoresis Capillary electrophoresis ( CE ) requires small sample volumes as well as small amounts of reagents and solvents . This makes it useful as an orthogonal technique for the analysis of samples available in small quantities and when using expensive reagents such as chiral selectors . In addition , short analysis times and high efficiency make it suitable for food analysis and foodomics . A review of articles published between February 2019 and February 2021 showed that CE methods have been applied for the analysis of amino acids , peptides , proteins , carbohydrates , lipids , vitamins , DNA , chiral compounds , food additives , pesticides , contaminants in fruits , vegetables , milk , meat and fish , as well as for foodomics.10 TECHNOLOGYNETWORKS.COM FOOD &amp; BEVERAGE ANALYSIS 19 Sensors The reduction of food quality due to spoilage is a major cause for concern in the food industry . This may be caused by changes in the physical and chemical characteristics of a foodstuff , or growth of undesirable microorganisms . To augment traditional methods of food monitoring , multisensory systems are deployed to detect food spoilage accurately and rapidly . These include : a. electronic noses to measure volatile compounds and detect off-odors b. electronic tongues for qualitative and quantitative analyses of complex multicomponent liquids c. biosensors for sensitive and selective detection of chemicals that indicate food spoilage , as well as contaminants11 Al Mughairy and Al-Lawati have reviewed several applications of microfluidic systems including labon-a chip , multifunctional tactile nano-layered aerogel sensors ( mTAS ) , lab-on-paper ( ? PADs ) and lab-on-a cloth coupled with chemiluminescence detection for the analysis of preservatives , pesticides , toxins , heavy metals , polyphenols , antioxidants and other nutrients in different foods and food products.12 Biosensors consist of biological detection systems in combination with a physical or chemical transducer . These convert biological , chemical or biochemical signals into measurable signals . Ali et al . reviewed numerous sensing technologies for the detection of pathogens in foodstuffs and their applications in food safety . For instance , adenosine triphosphate ( ATP ) - based bioluminescence sensors have been used to monitor the presence of microorganisms in meat and milk.13 Data analysis and chemometrics Kharbach et al have reviewed developments in spectroscopic techniques such as energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy ( EDXRF ) , hyperspectral and multispectral imaging , NMR , Raman , infrared ( IR ) , ultraviolet-visible ( UV-vis ) and fluorescence spectroscopies for food analysis . These non-destructive , rapid and economical methods are used not only to ascertain the quality of foodstuffs but to also determine the chemical composition , authenticity and detect contamination . The authors have further described the implementation of chemometric methods such as hierarchical cluster analysis ( HCA ) , principal component analysis ( PCA ) , linear discriminant analysis ( LDA ) , soft independent modeling of class analogy ( SIMCA ) , partial least squares-discriminant analysis ( PLS-DA ) , principal component regression ( PCR ) and partial least squares ( PLS ) to analyze the large sets of multidimensional spectral data obtained from complex food matrices . This approach provides valuable insights for both qualitative and quantitative analysis of food samples.14 Conclusions Although raw and processed foods can be complex matrices for analysis , a wide variety of techniques ranging from spectroscopy and chromatography to electrochemical and biological methods are available for rapid and accurate detection and quantification of both organic and inorganic analytes . The application of these techniques helps to ensure quality , safety and authenticity of food products for consumers and manufacturers as well as regulatory bodies . REFERENCES 1 .
